# Connections and open problems {#sec-outlook}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false title="Learning goals"}
- Place the results of this book in current research.
- Know the open problems.
:::

This closing chapter looks beyond the verdict of @sec-verdict. It relates the results of the book to active fields of research and lists the problems that remain open.

## Connections to current research {#sec-connections-current-research}

Read as statements about a non-unitary quantum field theory, these results connect to several active fields. The links are strongest for non-Hermitian physics and for resurgence. For both, the theorems above give exact field-theoretic examples of ideas that are mostly studied in quantum mechanics or in toy models. The connections below are our assessment, and the citations sample each field rather than survey it.

- **Non-Hermitian and $PT$-symmetric physics.** The transfer matrix is self-adjoint for a Krein form and commutes with an antilinear symmetry $\Theta$ (@thm-krein-transfer). So its spectrum is closed under complex conjugation, with $\Theta$-unbroken and $\Theta$-broken sectors (@sec-krein-unitarity). The Jordan blocks of the soliton fluctuation operators (@sec-semiclassics) are exceptional points, and @sec-unitarity (U4, U8) spells out what they imply. Pseudo-Hermiticity, $PT$ symmetry, Jordan forms and exceptional points are the organising concepts of non-Hermitian physics [@bender1998; @mostafazadeh2002; @ashida2020]. That field now spans photonics, open quantum systems and topological phases. With a boundary the corresponding questions are open. Does boundary unitarity become Krein pseudo-unitarity, and are the boundary spectra of $\Theta$-invariant boundaries (@prp-boundary-theta) real (@sec-boundary-open-problems, problem 7)?
- **Resurgence, Lefschetz thimbles and complex saddles.** The complex solitons are critical points of the thimble decomposition of the lattice integral (-@eq-lattice-action). Their one-loop determinants must be counted with algebraic multiplicity (Theorems [-@thm-jordan-chains] and [-@thm-hirota-factorization]). Intersection numbers decide which topological sectors contribute (@cnj-missing-charge). Resurgence relates perturbative data to the global structure of saddles in quantum mechanics and QFT [@witten2010; @dunne2015; @dunne2025].
- **The sign problem.** @thm-coulomb-gas turns a complex action into a positive Coulomb gas. This is a rare case where a complex weight is provably harmless. Complexifying field space by Picard–Lefschetz theory is a leading approach to sign problems such as QCD at finite density and the Hubbard model [@alexandru2022]. Here the answer is known exactly, which makes these theories a test case for those methods.
- **Constructive QFT and probability.** The continuum limit of @sec-continuum-limit is a statement about multi-species Coulomb gases and imaginary multiplicative chaos [@junnila2020; see also @lacoin2015 for complex chaos]. The conformal endpoint is now being built rigorously. Compactified imaginary Liouville CFT has been constructed and shown to satisfy the CFT axioms [@guillarmou2025], and the construction has been extended to higher-rank compactified imaginary Toda CFT [@yao2026]. Imaginary-coupling ATFT is this Toda theory perturbed by the vertex operator of the affine root.
- **S-matrix bootstrap and perturbative integrability.** Crossing and the bootstrap have a Hopf-algebraic origin [@delius1995]. Krein-unitarity replaces unitarity (Propositions [-@prp-krein-unitarity]–[-@prp-krein-fundamental]), and Hermitian analyticity is the missing condition for QFT unitarity [@miramontes1999]. The numerical S-matrix bootstrap explores the space of unitary two-dimensional S-matrices, with integrable models on its boundary [@paulos2017; @bercini2019]. The ladder of conditions in @sec-krein-unitarity raises the analogous question for Krein-unitary S-matrices. The numerical bootstrap has also been extended to reflection matrices [@kruczenski_murali2021]. The reflection amplitudes of Part VII, with their boundary bound states (@sec-boundary-bound-states), give exact data for such studies.
- **Non-unitary and complex CFTs.** RSOS restrictions give non-unitary minimal models of Lee–Yang type. These models distinguish the effective central charge from the central charge, and their complex finite-volume spectra are seen in the truncated conformal space approach (@sec-unitary-subtheories and @sec-unitarity, U5–U7). Complex CFTs control walking renormalization-group flows and weakly first-order transitions such as the $Q>4$ Potts model [@gorbenko2018; @gorbenko2018b]. @cnj-unitary-rsos would give a criterion, checkable from the S-matrix, for when a restricted model is unitary.
- **ODE/IM, exact WKB and gauge/string theory.** The linear problems of ATFT underlie the massive ODE/IM correspondence [@lukyanov2010; @dorey2013]. The ultraviolet limit of the $A_r$ massive ODE/IM correspondence gives non-unitary $WA_r$ minimal models [@ito_shu2018]. A recent monograph reviews these correspondences, with applications to exact WKB, minimal surfaces and gluon amplitudes in AdS/CFT [@ito_shu2025].
- **$q$-deformed world-sheet theories.** IRF bases restore unitarity of $q$-deformed S-matrices [@hoare2013]. This is the mechanism we propose for unitary restrictions of ATFT, and we confirm it for the kinks of $a_2^{(1)}$, where it works exactly for $p'\equiv\pm1\pmod p$ (@prp-rsos-kinks).
- **Integrable circuits and analogue simulation.** The light-cone regularization of @prp-krein-regularization is a brickwork circuit of R-matrix gates. It is unitary for a Krein form rather than for the Hilbert-space inner product. The zero-mode model of @sec-solvable-check and few-site versions of this circuit are small enough that complex-conjugate level pairs and exceptional points could be realised in $PT$-symmetric photonic or cold-atom systems [@ashida2020]. This link is more speculative than the others.

The half-line theory of Part VII has connections of its own. They run through two objects that are now studied well beyond boundary field theory: the boundary state (-@eq-boundary-state) and the coideal subalgebras that survive the boundary (@sec-coideal).

- **Quantum symmetric pairs and $\imath$quantum groups.** The coideals of @sec-boundary-qg are quantum symmetric pairs (@sec-qsp). These arose independently in harmonic analysis on quantum symmetric spaces [@noumi1996; @letzter1999] and as the symmetry of boundary scattering [@delius_mackay2003]. They are now the subject of a theory of $\imath$quantum groups, with its own canonical bases, Schur dualities and Kazhdan–Lusztig theory [@bao_wang2018; @wang2023]. Its universal K-matrices yield solutions of the reflection equation [@balagovic_kolb2019; @appel_vlaar2022; @appel_vlaar2025]. Part VII gives this theory a physical test. For $a_n^{(1)}$ with $n\ge2$, a vector reflection matrix with non-zero coideal parameters needs $\hat\epsilon_j^2=\epsilon_*^2$ (@prp-an-k-existence). These parameters lie outside Kolb's parameter set, and the coideals they define are character twists of the standard one (@sec-letzter-kolb). By @cnj-neumann-coideal one of them belongs to the Neumann boundary. So a boundary condition as simple as Neumann needs a coideal outside Kolb's framework, of the kind that Baseilhac and Belliard and Regelskis and Vlaar admit [@baseilhac_belliard2010; @regelskis_vlaar2016]. Two questions are open: whether these coideals have a universal K-matrix [@regelskis_vlaar2016, Rem. 9.2], and whether coideals exhaust the integrable boundaries (@sec-boundary-open-problems, problem 5).
- **Integrable boundary states, quenches and defect CFT.** The boundary state (-@eq-boundary-state) is built from pairs of particles with opposite rapidities, with pair amplitude $K(\frac{i\pi}2-\theta)$, and it is annihilated by the parity-odd charges $Q_s-Q_{-s}$. Piroli, Pozsgay and Vernier took this last property as the definition of an integrable initial state for quantum quenches in spin chains [@piroli2017]. Integrable matrix product states then correspond to operator-valued solutions of a twisted reflection equation, and the explicit solutions are labelled by symmetric pairs and represent twisted Yangians [@pozsgay2019]. In AdS/CFT, one-point functions in defect CFTs are overlaps of Bethe states with such states [@deleeuw2015]. Their K-matrices are fixed by an unbroken symmetry that forms a symmetric pair with the full symmetry [@gombor_bajnok2020]. This is the structure that Delius, MacKay and Short found for rational reflection matrices [@dms2001; @mackay_short2003], and @sec-boundary-qg is its trigonometric form. The K-matrices of @sec-soliton-reflection and @sec-qsp should therefore give integrable initial states for the $U_q(\hat g)$ chains of open problem 8. The exact g-function (@sec-boundary-finite-size) is the field-theory analogue of the exact overlap formulas.
- **Boundary sine-Gordon in quantum circuits.** With a free massless bulk, the boundary cosine of @sec-bsg-classical alone is still integrable. It describes tunnelling between quantum Hall edges, where integrability gives the exact conductance [@fls1995]. At low energies it also describes a Josephson junction at the end of a transmission line, whose dissipative Schmid–Bulgadaev transition was disputed for decades [@murani2020]. The transition has now been observed by scattering microwave photons off the junction [@kuzmin2025], so the measured quantities are boundary reflection probabilities, elastic and inelastic. Chains of Josephson junctions have been proposed as simulators of the massive bulk theory [@roy2021]. Ended by a junction, such a chain would realise the massive boundary theory of @sec-boundary-sine-gordon, with its boundary bound states and their reflection amplitudes. Like the circuit link above, this one is speculative.
- **Constructive boundary field theory.** The UV–IR relation (@cnj-bsg-uv-ir) decides where $\hat\epsilon=0$ lies, and with it open problem 12 of @sec-boundary-open-problems. At $\phi_0=0$ the relation follows from the boundary energy and an expectation value that Fateev, Zamolodchikov and Zamolodchikov obtained from boundary Liouville theory [@bpt2002, sec. 3.5]. The structure constants of boundary Liouville CFT have since been derived in its probabilistic construction [@ang_remy_sun2025; @ang_remy_sun_zhu2023]. These results are at real coupling and concern the conformal theory, so they establish the input of that derivation but not the relation itself. In the other direction, the constructive continuum limit of Part IX is taken between Dirichlet walls (@sec-collapse-thresholds). Whether these walls are integrable boundaries of the imaginary-coupling theory is open problem 7 of @sec-boundary-open-problems.


The defects of Part VIII connect to three further subjects. Their open problems are listed in @sec-defect-open-problems.

- **Defects in spin chains and quantum circuits.** The transmission matrices of @sec-defect-qg are L-operators of a Borel subalgebra on an infinite-dimensional defect space, and the same objects define integrable defects in the XXZ chain [@weston2010] and equivalences between spin models [@bajnok2006]. A Trotterized integrable chain is a brickwork circuit of two-site gates, and an integrable defect becomes a column of gates acting on an extra degree of freedom. Such circuits would be a natural place to simulate defect transmission and the unstable defect states of @sec-sg-defect-spectrum and @sec-an-defect-bound-states. This link too is speculative.
- **Defects in AdS/CFT.** One-point functions in the defect CFTs of AdS/CFT are overlaps with integrable boundary states [@deleeuw2015], and the doubling trick (@sec-doubling-trick) turns every transmitting defect into a boundary of a doubled theory. For the defects of this part, the unbroken symmetry of that boundary is a pair of Borel halves, not a twisted diagonal coideal (@sec-defect-boundary). Which symmetry a transmitting interface preserves in those settings is open.
- **Bäcklund transformations and Q-operators.** The type-I defects are Bäcklund transformations frozen at a point (@sec-backlund, @sec-defect-backlund-an), and their defect operators over Fock modules are Q-operators (@sec-q-operators) [@blz1997; @rossi_weston2002]. In lattice models solved by the Yang–Baxter equation, Q-operators have long been read as quantum Bäcklund transformations, so defects put the classical and the quantum notion in one frame. Which other models with a Borel L-operator have defects of this kind, and what those defects are classically, is open.

These connections suggest where the results can be used. First, Theorems [-@thm-bounded-weight]–[-@thm-vacuum-energy] use neither integrability nor the Lie-algebraic data, beyond the non-negativity of the fugacities (@sec-definition). So they give a template for other theories with periodic complex potentials, such as complex Liouville and Toda CFTs and their deformations. Second, the open problems of @sec-open-problems are natural targets for these communities. The thimble intersection numbers (problem 4) can be attacked with the algorithms reviewed in [@alexandru2022]. The missing soliton S-matrices (problem 2) could be constrained by extending the on-shell loop methods of [@polvara2023; @fabri_polvara2024] to non-simply-laced algebras and imaginary coupling. The $\Theta$-broken sectors (problems 6 and 8) can be mapped numerically with the truncated conformal space approach, tensor networks and the lattice of @prp-krein-regularization. The infinite-volume limit and mass gap (@cnj-correlation-range) might be reached by adding the affine perturbation to the probabilistic constructions above, using Theorems [-@thm-coulomb-gas], [-@thm-below-2pi] and [-@thm-window] as input. The open problems of the half-line (@sec-boundary-open-problems) are targets in the same way. The completeness of the coideals and their universal K-matrices (problem 5) are questions for the theory of quantum symmetric pairs. The conjectured particle amplitudes (problems 2 and 3) can be tested with the boundary TBA and the truncated conformal space approach (@sec-boundary-finite-size), as Ahn, Kim and Rim did for the Neumann boundary [@akr2002].

## Open problems {#sec-open-problems}

The problems below concern the theory on the full line. Those of the half-line are listed in @sec-boundary-open-problems, and two of them meet problems below; those of defects are listed in @sec-defect-open-problems. The missing boundary vacua (problem 6 there) may come from the complex two-soliton configurations of problem 4. The non-unitary half-line (problem 7 there) asks the questions of problems 1 and 5 with a boundary.

1. The infinite-volume limit and mass gap (@cnj-correlation-range), using multi-species Coulomb-gas methods. This includes the claim that only vacuum-energy counterterms are needed in the bulk for simply-laced algebras, and the counterterms needed at and above $\beta^2_{\rm UV}$. In finite volume the continuum limit is now proved below $\beta^2_{\rm UV}$ for every algebra (Theorems [-@thm-below-2pi] and [-@thm-window]), awaiting independent check. @thm-cluster-bound gives the stability bound $\sup_a\log\Xi_a(z)\le A(1+z^{1/(1-\kappa)})$, with the exponent dictated by the bulk free energy (@lem-stability). A natural first step towards infinite volume is a version of @thm-cluster-bound at fixed physical coupling, with a constant per unit area that is uniform in the volume. Theorems [-@thm-nn-distances] and [-@thm-cluster-bound] would also benefit from an independent referee's check.
2. Exact soliton S-matrices. @sec-sm-introduction supplies the lowest solitons of $c_n^{(1)}$, $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$ and $e_6^{(2)}$. Still open are $f_4^{(1)}$, where the scalar factor of the $\mathbf{27}$ amplitude is not known, the remaining soliton species, and general $n$ (the S-matrices are verified for $n\le4$; their R-matrices are known for all $n$ [@dgz1994; @dgz1996]). The one-loop results of @sec-one-loop-masses-folded constrain them. They give the floating Coxeter number of the soliton masses for every folded algebra, for example $H=2n-\beta^2/4\pi+O(\beta^4)$ for $c_n^{(1)}$, and the exceptional points predict pairs of nearby poles. For $f_4^{(1)}$ they predict the Corrigan–Dorey–Sasaki soliton mass pattern with $H_s=12+3\beta^2/4\pi$, while the breathers have $H_b=12-3\beta^2/4\pi$. So the assumption of Part VI that soliton and breather fusion angles coincide fails for $f_4^{(1)}$, as it does for Takács's $g_2^{(1)}$ amplitude. The one-loop masses select different integer lifts (@sec-one-loop-masses-folded), but with them the lowest-breather amplitude still does not match. A construction that ties the solitons to $H_s$ and the breathers to $H_b$ separately, as Takács's $g_2^{(1)}$ amplitude does, is the natural next attempt. Two routes avoid the missing S-matrices. The nested Bethe ansatz of the lattice models of open problem 8 gives finite-volume levels and multi-particle transfer-matrix eigenvalues directly, which is all the $\Theta$-breaking criterion of @sec-krein-unitarity uses. For $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$ the lattice mass ratios of [@vernier2016] agree with Part VI's masses for every $n$ and every coupling in their regime I (@sec-a2n-lattice). This confirms the S-matrix masses but does not test the counting rule. The $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$ solitons fold single $d_{2n}^{(1)}$ solitons. These have only simple zeros (@sec-one-loop-masses-folded), so algebraic and geometric multiplicities coincide there. A lattice test of the counting rule needs a staggered vertex model whose scaling limit is $c_n^{(1)}$ or $b_n^{(1)}$ Toda; by the pattern of @sec-a2n-lattice these are the $U_q(c_n^{(1)})$ and $U_q(b_n^{(1)})$ models (open problem 8).
3. @cnj-counting-rule in general. The counting rule is Theorems [-@thm-jordan-chains] and [-@thm-hirota-factorization] and @prp-net-count. @prp-hirota-form gives (H) for every static soliton of a simply-laced algebra and for every folding, given the degree bound (D), and @sec-one-loop-masses-folded checks the mass-ratio statement numerically in every family. The open parts are:
   - **The degree bound.** Prove (D) for all ranks, presumably through the nilpotency $(F^a)^{n_j+1}=0$ on $L(\Lambda_j)$.
   - **Threshold weights.** Give a general theory of the trace weight at threshold resonances. These are not special to folding: simple zeros of $X_{ab}$ sit at other channels' thresholds in $a_n^{(1)}$ ($h$ even), $d_n^{(1)}$ ($n$ odd) and $e_6^{(1)}$, and double zeros do so in $b_n^{(1)}$, $c_n^{(1)}$ and $f_4^{(1)}$ (@sec-hirota-form-dn1-en1).
   - **Jordan types without (R).** Prove that the Jordan types equal the individual orders where (R) fails away from thresholds, as in $b_n^{(1)}$, $g_2^{(1)}$ and $f_4^{(1)}$; numerically they do, for example type $(3,1)$ at $\lambda=\tfrac32$ in $g_2^{(1)}$.
   - **Spectral singularities.** Static solitons have none (@prp-hirota-form). They can occur only for moving or breather backgrounds in $\Theta$-broken sectors.
   - **The mass ratio.** Prove it, and explain why the Lie-dual particle masses appear at $\beta_r^2=+\beta^2$ for untwisted algebras and the theory's own particle masses at $-\beta^2$ for twisted ones.
   - **The one-loop mass.** @prp-net-count part 2 and @prp-one-loop-mass are theorems about the Mellin form (-@eq-one-loop-mellin). Two inputs remain. Prove the root location of @prp-hirota-form part 3 for $d_n^{(1)}$, $e_n^{(1)}$ and the foldings, and prove that (-@eq-one-loop-mellin) is the continuum limit of the lattice Gaussian of @prp-thimble-gaussian.
4. @cnj-missing-charge. The reduced static model of @sec-which-saddles-contribute computes thimble intersection numbers and validates the method. It cannot decide the conjecture, because for $a_3^{(1)}$ no static saddle of energy $M_2$ carries the four missing weights of $\Lambda^2$. What is needed is the decomposition of a $(1+1)$-dimensional lattice sector with Dirichlet data $0$ and $2\pi\vec\lambda/\beta$. Are complexified two-soliton bound states at the fusing angle critical points there, and are their $\nu_\sigma$ nonzero in the missing sectors? The algorithms reviewed in [@alexandru2022] apply directly.
5. A proof of Krein asymptotic completeness, completing @prp-krein-unitarity. For the fundamental solitons of $a_n^{(1)}$ the conclusion of @prp-krein-unitarity holds exactly, without it (@prp-krein-fundamental). So it does for their antisolitons, since the soliton–antisoliton amplitudes are Krein-unitary with the same, untwisted colour reversal (@prp-boundary-krein, part 1). The direct route extends to any S-matrix whose R-matrix satisfies the Hermiticity and colour-reversal identities of @prp-krein-fundamental. The open cases are the fused and non-simply-laced R-matrices of Part VI. Which multi-soliton sectors of $a_n^{(1)}$ are broken is a separate question. Three solitons with three colours are broken at every $q$ sampled, four with three colours are unbroken exactly when $\operatorname{Re}q<-\frac12$, and near $q=-1$ a parity rule for the colour multiplicities decides (@sec-krein-unitarity). Neither the window nor the rule is proved.
6. The sector classification for self-conjugate theories. Soliton–breather sectors are unbroken, with any number of breathers, whenever the breather amplitudes have the block form (@prp-scalar-breathers); this holds in every self-conjugate case computed in Part VI. Soliton–excited-soliton sectors are broken wherever an excited soliton at an odd tower level exists, because their R-part is $\check R(-z)$. In the Bloch sector $\alpha=0$, which every bosonic global form contains, the fundamental multi-soliton sectors are broken too: the spinor two-soliton amplitudes of $c_n^{(1)}$ and $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$ outside a narrow rapidity window, and the $N$-kink sectors of $a_2^{(2)}$ for $\lvert\psi\rvert>\pi/N$ (@sec-sector-status). What remains:
   - **Bloch sectors.** A grading of the exchange of soliton labels is a Bloch twist (@prp-exchange-twist), and the global form fixes which twists occur (@prp-bloch-sectors). Changing the sign of $q$, which the crossing test of @sec-crossing-sign detects, is a Bloch twist too: for $N$ spinor solitons it shifts $\alpha$ by $\pi N(1,\dots,1)$, up to a phase in each sector. The sector $Q=0$, $\alpha=0$, where the bosonic breaking appears, exists in every bosonic form; whether $a_2^{(2)}$ admits a fermionic form, which would replace it by $\alpha=\pi$, is open. What remains is the classification as a function of $\alpha$: a proof of the two-kink threshold of @sec-sector-status, the broken islands at intermediate $\alpha$ for $N\ge3$, and an explanation of why the threshold for $\lvert\psi\rvert\ge2\pi/3$ is the quantum-trace twist $q^{\pm2m}$ of the RSOS restriction. A twisted light-cone Izergin–Korepin chain (open problem 8) would test @prp-bloch-sectors for $a_2^{(2)}$ directly.
   - **The $\pi/N$ rule.** Prove it, perhaps through the signature of the $U_q$-invariant Hermitian form on $V^{\otimes N}$ at $\lvert q\rvert=1$.
   - **Remaining amplitudes.** The $e_6^{(2)}$, $d_4^{(3)}$ and $g_2^{(1)}$ soliton sectors, and the excited solitons of $c_3^{(1)}$, whose towers have half-integer spacing.
7. Hermitian-analytic (IRF) bases beyond the $su(2)$-type cases of [@hoare2013]. For the fundamental kinks of $a_2^{(1)}$ the answer is @prp-rsos-kinks: such a basis exists if and only if $p'\equiv\pm1\pmod p$. So $\Theta$-unbroken sectors need not admit one; the $W_3(p,p+2)$ kink sectors are examples. Three questions remain. (a) The criterion for $U_q(\widehat{sl}_n)$ with $n\ge4$ and for other algebras, which needs fused face weights; the necessity argument of @prp-rsos-kinks already works for vector kinks at any rank. (b) A proof that the $p'=p+2$ kink sectors are unbroken at every particle number, and an explanation of why $p'-p=2$ is special. (c) The Krein form behind the exact $(s,1/\bar s)$ pairs of the restricted theory, and its relation to that of @prp-krein-fundamental.
8. Integrable lattice regularizations: light-cone (staggered) $U_q$ vertex models [@destri1987; @reshetikhin1994], with Bethe-ansatz control of the scaling limit through non-linear integral equations [@destri1992; @destri1995; @zinnjustin1998 for untwisted simply-laced $\hat g$]. Doikou and Nepomechie [-@doikou1999] identify the hole S-matrix of the critical $A_{N-1}^{(1)}$ chain with the $a_{N-1}^{(1)}$ soliton S-matrix. Matching their S-matrix parameter $e^{i\pi/(\nu-1)}$, $\nu=\pi/\mu$, with @sec-imaginary-coupling-vacua shows that for $a_{N-1}^{(1)}$ the lattice anisotropy $q=e^{i\mu}$ corresponds to $\beta^2=4(\pi-\mu)$; for $N=2$ this is the Destri–de Vega relation $\beta_{\rm SG}^2=8(\pi-\mu)$. @thm-below-2pi's range is then $\mu>\pi/2$, the attractive regime, and @thm-window extends it to $\mu>\pi/N$. The window is $\pi/N<\mu\le\pi/2$, and the neutral thresholds of @sec-collapse-thresholds, the poles of the exact bulk energy, sit at $q^{kN}=-1$. The light-cone evolution is exactly Krein-unitary (@prp-krein-regularization).

   Three questions precede any use as a definition. (i) Which algebra and which regime. [@vernier2016] obtain imaginary $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$ Toda from the $U_q(a_{2n-1}^{(2)})$ chain. This suggests that the lattice carries $U_q(\hat g)$ and that $\hat g^\vee$ appears only in the continuum S-matrix, with a renormalized $q$ (@sec-a2n-lattice). For $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$ the renormalization is explicit: the lattice has $q=e^{i\gamma}$ and the soliton S-matrix $q=e^{-i\pi^2/2\gamma}$ (-@eq-q-physical). The same R-matrix also has non-Toda continuum limits in other regimes. (ii) The ground-state structure, which [@zinnjustin1998; @doikou1999] assume and which is subtle for twisted algebras. Rigorous Bethe-ansatz tools exist so far only for six-vertex models [@duminil2022], that is for $a_1^{(1)}$, where the window is empty. The Euclidean weights carry phases, so Theorems [-@thm-coulomb-gas] and [-@thm-vacuum-energy] have no evident counterpart (@prp-krein-regularization, checks). (iii) The comparison with @sec-continuum-limit. The lattice has periodic boundary conditions and constant coupling, while @thm-below-2pi's theory has the coupling profile of @sec-wick-ordering-statement. The natural target is a bridge theorem: for $0<\beta^2<2\pi$, the vacuum energy given by the non-linear integral equations on a circle of length $L_t$ equals $-\lim_{L_x\to\infty}L_x^{-1}\log\Xi$, where far from the walls the coupling is constant. This needs a crossed-channel version of @sec-hamiltonian-structure-krein-space, with the spatial zero mode compactified as in @sec-solvable-check.

   In finite volume this route is no longer needed for existence below $\beta^2_{\rm UV}$ (@thm-window). What it can supply is the bulk energy and its singularities across the window (@sec-collapse-thresholds), finite-volume form factors through the quantum inverse problem [@hegedus2017], and the data missing in problem 2.

## Exercises {#sec-outlook-exercises}

::: {#exr-open-problem}
Choose one of the open problems of @sec-open-problems and write a one-page research plan: what would be computed or proved, which chapters of this book provide the tools, and what would count as a solution.
:::

## Notes and references {#sec-outlook-notes}

The connections to current research are surveyed with representative references in @sec-connections-current-research.
